subject: DB38CEAE0E40EAE9C4AAFC8ADE5D2C13
introduction: Most of these readings are remarks of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá about a mountain He lived beside: its air and views, its decline and promise, the places where Bahá’u’lláh’s tent stood, and the people who settled there to wait for a promised one and did not know Him when He came. Carmel was already a mountain of scripture, Elijah’s mountain and Isaiah’s image of beauty, so the Hebrew prophets are its natural company, with the Gospels on tents, mountains and unrecognized visits.
questions: Isaiah, Amos and the Song of Songs each use Carmel as an image. What does the mountain stand for in each, and which of these meanings do the readings take up?
A prisoner pitches his tent “with glory” on the mountain. How do the tabernacle of Moses and the psalmist’s pavilion help in hearing what a tent means here?
Settlers wrote over their doors that the Beloved would come, and monks refused to hear a message. What do the verses from John and Luke suggest about why nearness does not bring recognition?
In the last readings stones soar, trees cry out and Nature laments. How do Isaiah and Paul speak of the creation’s part in such a day?

outside.why: The mountain is wrapped in “the white mantle of spirituality”. Isaiah made its beauty a figure of the day of God: the excellency of Carmel and Sharon, they shall see the glory of the Lord.
The air and the panorama are praised as vitalizing. The psalmist looks at hills for more than air: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
Carmel’s prosperity “declined into ruin”. Amos opens his book with that decline as a judgment: the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither.

The reading expects the ruined place to prosper again. Shelley’s traveller sees only what time does to greatness: nothing beside remains, and the lone and level sands stretch far away. What makes a ruin a promise in one telling and a warning in the other?
A prisoner “pitched His tent with glory”. In Exodus the place of meeting with God is also a tent, and it stands outside: Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp.
The tent “has been raised on this Holy ground”. The psalmist uses the same words for where God shelters him: in his pavilion, in the secret of his tabernacle, upon a rock.
“The pavilion of the Lord will be pitched on the mountain”. The Revelation of John ends with the same figure made universal: behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them.
The feast kept on the mountain remembers Elijah’s ascent. The Second Book of Kings: there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Monks living on the mountain of prophecy would neither see the messenger nor read the message. John’s prologue: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
“How many prophets longed to be here in these days of God.” Jesus to his disciples: many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them.

The settlers wrote over their doors that the Beloved would come, while He lived at the foot of their hill. John the Baptist told those who questioned him: there standeth one among you, whom ye know not.
Prophets “always went into the wilderness to pray”, and many walked on Carmel. Luke says of Jesus that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.

On another high mountain Peter saw Jesus transfigured, with Moses and Elias, and offered to build three tabernacles and stay. The Gospel has them go down again. What is a holy mountain for, if not to be stayed on?

Syria is “a world in miniature”, with the trees of hot and cold climates together. Deuteronomy describes the same country to those about to enter it: a land of brooks of water, of wheat and barley, vines, fig trees and pomegranates.
Carmel is longed for as “the garden of the Lord”. The Song of Solomon reaches for the mountain when it wants a word for beauty: thine head upon thee is like Carmel.

At the revelation on Carmel “the stones soared, the trees cried out”. Isaiah promised such a day: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.

Nature is heard crying in the nights and moaning at dawn. Paul hears the same sound and takes it for expectation: the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.

psalm-in-his-pavilion.text: For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock

luke-prophets-and-kings-have-desired.text: Blessed are the eyes which see the things that ye see: For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them; and to hear those things which ye hear, and have not heard them

matthew-three-tabernacles.text: And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him. Then answered Peter, and said unto Jesus, Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias

exodus-tabernacle-without-the-camp.text: And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp

song-head-like-carmel.text: Thine head upon thee is like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king is held in the galleries

amos-top-of-carmel-shall-wither.text: And he said, The Lord will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither

deuteronomy-land-of-wheat-and-barley.text: For the Lord thy God bringeth thee into a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills; A land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of oil olive, and honey; A land wherein thou shalt eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass
